sections.text:
Paul is angry, and it shows from the start. He is amazed that the Galatians are so quickly deserting the one who called them. Teachers had told the non-Jewish believers in Galatia that they must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. Paul answers that this would abandon the good news itself: people are made right with God through faith in Christ, not by works of the law.

He asks them, with open frustration, whether they received the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith. He appeals to his own story, to Abraham who believed before the law was given, and to the Galatians' own experience of the Spirit.

Then comes the other side. Freedom in Christ is not license. It shows itself in love and in the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control.
Galatia was a region in what is now Turkey. Whether Paul wrote to churches in its north or its south is debated, and with it the date, between about 48 and 55. It may be his earliest letter.

Galatians was central to the Reformation. In recent decades scholars have debated what Paul means by works of the law: any effort to earn God's favor, or the particular marks that set Jews apart, such as circumcision and food laws. Readers also compare Paul's teaching here with James 2 and generally find the two address different errors.

Paul does not begin with a thank-you. After a short greeting he comes straight out: “I marvel that you are so quickly deserting him who called you” Some are troubling the churches of Galatia with a different message, and Paul says there is no other good news. Even an angel from heaven who preached another would be cursed.

So he tells how he came to the message. It was not taught him by anyone; “it came to me through revelation of Jesus Christ.” He recalls his old life: zealous for the traditions of his fathers, and a persecutor of the assembly of God. Then God called him, and he went away into Arabia, and returned to Damascus. Only after three years did he go up to Jerusalem, to meet Peter for fifteen days, and he saw James, the Lord's brother.

The churches of Judea only heard that the one who had persecuted them was “now preaches the faith that he once tried to destroy”. And they glorified God in him.

Paul writes to churches in Galatia. Scholars differ on whether this means the north or the south of the region, and so on the date; the letter is usually dated somewhere between the late 40s and the mid 50s. The word translated cursed is strong. For the story of Paul's call see Acts 9, 22 and 26. The point of the chapter is that his message came from God, not from the apostles in Jerusalem.

Fourteen years later, Paul says, he went up again to Jerusalem, with Barnabas and with Titus, a Greek. He set the Good News he preached to the Gentiles before those who were respected. Titus was not compelled to be circumcised. James, Cephas and John gave Barnabas and Paul “the right hand of fellowship”, and asked only that they remember the poor.

Then the story turns to a hard moment in Antioch. Peter had been eating with the Gentiles, but when some came from James he drew back. Even Barnabas was carried away. Paul says, “I resisted him to his face,” and said it before them all.

The chapter closes on the core of his argument. A person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ. Paul says he has been crucified with Christ, and that Christ lives in him. If righteousness came by the law, Christ died for nothing.

Paul writes to churches in Galatia to defend the Good News he preached. Scholars differ on whether the Jerusalem visit is the one in Acts 15 or an earlier one. The phrase translated faith in Jesus Christ can also be read as the faithfulness of Christ, and Christians differ on this. Paul and Peter are both Jews, and the question was whether Gentile believers must live as Jews do.

Paul loses patience, and his love shows in it. “Foolish Galatians,” he says, and asks who has bewitched them, when Jesus Christ was portrayed before their eyes as crucified. He asks a simple question: did they receive the Spirit by works of the law, or by hearing with faith?

He goes back to Abraham, who believed God, and says that those who are of faith are his children. The law brings a curse on those who do not keep all of it, but “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law”. Paul argues that the promise to Abraham came four hundred thirty years before the law, so the law does not cancel it.

Then why the law? It was added until the promised offspring came, and it was like a tutor leading to Christ. The chapter ends with a wide embrace. All who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ, and “you are all one in Christ Jesus”.

Paul writes to churches in Galatia, who were being told that Gentile believers must keep the law of Moses. He draws on Genesis 12 and 15, Habakkuk 2, Leviticus 18 and Deuteronomy 21. Christians differ on how verse 28 bears on the roles of men and women in the church. Paul is a Jew arguing about the place of the law in the plan of God, and this chapter has been misused to disparage Judaism.

Paul pictures a child who will one day inherit everything, and until then lives like a servant under guardians. That was how it was, he says, until “the fullness of the time came, God sent out his Son”, born under the law, to redeem those under the law. Because they are God's children, God sent the Spirit of his Son into their hearts, crying “Abba, Father!”

Then he turns to the Galatians themselves, and he sounds like a worried parent. Why turn back to what is weak and miserable? He reminds them how they received him when he was ill, and how they would have given their very eyes. He calls them his little children, in labor again “until Christ is formed in you”.

Finally he tells a story from their own law, of Abraham's two sons, one by a servant and one by a free woman. He calls it an allegory, of two covenants, and says that believers are children of promise.

Paul writes to churches in Galatia who were drawn to the law of Moses. The story of the two sons is in Genesis 16 and 21, and the quotation in verse 27 is from Isaiah 54. Paul himself calls it an allegory. The contrast between two covenants has been misused to demean Jews. Christians differ on what the elemental principles of verse 3 are, whether spiritual powers or basic teachings.

The chapter begins like a shout. “Stand firm therefore in the liberty by which Christ has made us free”. Paul warns that if the Galatians take up circumcision as a way to be right with God, Christ will profit them nothing. What counts is “faith working through love”. He regrets that someone has interfered, for they were running well, and a little yeast grows through the whole lump.

His answer to freedom is not license. They were called to freedom, and the whole law is fulfilled in one word: love your neighbor as yourself. If they bite and devour each other, they will consume one another.

He sets the flesh against the Spirit, lists the deeds of the flesh, and then paints the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control. “Against such things there is no law.”

Paul writes to churches in Galatia, where some were pressing Gentile believers to be circumcised. The command in verse 14 comes from Leviticus 19. Verse 12 is a harsh line, and translators and readers take it in different ways. The list of the deeds of the flesh includes sexual sins, and the chapter says what the text says about them without sorting people. For the Spirit's work see also Romans 8.

The letter turns to everyday life in a community. If someone is caught in a fault, those who are spiritual should restore that person in gentleness, watching that they are not tempted themselves. “Bear one another’s burdens,” Paul writes, and so fulfill the law of Christ. A few lines later he adds that each one will bear his own load, and the two sit side by side.

He uses the picture of a field. Whatever a person sows, they will also reap. “Let’s not be weary in doing good,” he says, because in due season there is a harvest if we don't give up. We should do good toward all, and especially toward the household of the faith.

Then he takes the pen himself and writes in large letters. He warns again about circumcision, and says he will boast only in the cross. What matters is a new creation. He ends: “I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus branded on my body.”

Paul writes to churches in Galatia. Many readers think that in verse 11 Paul takes the pen from a secretary and writes the closing lines himself. The phrase God's Israel in verse 16 is read in different ways: as the church, as believing Jews, or as the whole people of God, and Christians differ. For sowing and reaping compare 2 Corinthians 9.
